summary: I checked the message lifecycle and the wake schedule in the current code (journal.py, envelope.py, views.py, trajectory.py) against all 23 persisted runs in artifacts/simulations_v4, simulations_v3 and matched_pairs (922 wakes, 700 wake firings, 280 observation transitions). The observation half is genuinely sound: observation is an append-only transition on the same item, no committed record is ever rewritten, mark_observed cannot reach a non-recipient, wake reasons never leak to the person woken, every wake carries a concrete reason, and all 922 wakes satisfy now < due <= cutoff. The scheduling half is not. I confirm the prior reviewer: only world_process and actor_plan are ever scheduled, and because each is hard-coded at its single call site, provenance is a restatement of which line scheduled the wake rather than a check on anything. The cost is concrete and visible in the newest corpus: provenance is never consulted at fire time, so a world_process wake is never routed back to the world, 27% of all wake firings degenerate into a content-free actor poke, and simulations_v4/case1_cold_email still answers NO over a 336-hour window having simulated five minutes -- the exact defect trajectory.py:872-885 claims was fixed.

findings.title: Three of the five declared wake provenances are unreachable, so provenance checks nothing
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:154-158 declares WAKE_PROVENANCE = (actor_plan, observed_event, world_process, known_deadline, action_completion). There are exactly two _schedule_wake call sites and each hard-codes its label: trajectory.py:395-397 (provenance="world_process") and trajectory.py:535-538 (provenance="actor_plan"). Confirmed in the data: 922 wakes across artifacts/simulations_v4 (270), simulations_v3 (572) and matched_pairs (80) are 547 world_process and 375 actor_plan; observed_event, known_deadline and action_completion appear zero times. The two guards that are supposed to catch this are set-membership tests and therefore pass tautologically: evaluation/verify_run.py:90-92 and tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1591-1595.
findings.why_it_matters: Provenance is a 1:1 function of the call site, so it can never be wrong and can never discriminate a grounded wake from a poll -- the invariant 'every wake has a valid provenance' is true by construction and proves nothing. The three dead members are not cosmetic. known_deadline was the designed mechanism for bringing a person back as their own deadline nears (SEMANTIC_RUNTIME_COMPLETION_PLAN.md:239-247); without it the only things that ever return an actor to a situation are their own last plan and whatever the world happened to ask for, which is why six of nine v4 runs have their last committed event inside the first hour of a 56-336 hour window. observed_event and action_completion were replaced by direct actor_step calls (trajectory.py:664-678, 703-704) that carry no provenance at all, so those consultations are invisible to grounded_wakes.jsonl and to verify_run.py.
findings.suggested_fix: Either wire the three missing provenances (a known_deadline wake derived from bindings['cutoff'] for any actor with an unfinished commitment; observed_event and action_completion as real queue entries rather than inline actor_step calls) or delete them from the vocabulary, and replace the membership assertion in verify_run.py and test_semantic_runtime.py:1591 with one that asserts every declared member is actually produced somewhere in the corpus.

findings.title: A world_process wake is never routed back to the world; 192 of 700 firings are content-free actor pokes
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:957-993. At fire time ev.data['provenance'] is read only to pop the pending key (lines 961-962); it never influences handling. The branch that re-consults the world (world_step(trigger_kind='pending_progression'), line 979) is gated on journal.available_unobserved(aid) being non-empty; when it is empty the code falls through to a bare actor_step(aid, cause=fired) at line 993. Measured over every ledger.jsonl in the three corpora: 192 of 700 wake firings (27%) had nothing pending. It is 100% of firings in simulations_v4/{case1_cold_email, b1_r2, b2_r1, b2_r2} and matched_pairs/{b1_okafor_herrera, b1_okafor_herrera__r3, b1_okafor_herrera__r4, b2_thornbury_lim, b2_thornbury_lim__r2}. Worked example, simulations_v4/case1_cold_email: world_judgments.jsonl call c1 returns event=null ("the email is simply traveling") plus a wake on mark_cuban at +5 minutes reasoned "The email may have arrived in Mark's inbox; check if he notices it." The starting event e11 in journal.jsonl has for=["jordan_reyes"] (compiled_scene.json starting_events[0].visible_to = ["Jordan Reyes"]), and 'for' is write-once -- journal.py:49-68 sets it at commit and journal.py:70-99 only ever appends observers -- so available_unobserved('mark_cuban') is permanently empty. The wake fired at 14:05, the world was never asked whether the email arrived, and mark_cuban's rendered view (trajectory.md) reads "(you have not observed anything yet)" plus "time has passed and you are looking at your situation again". runtime_metrics.json: steps 1, committed_events 1, answer NO_AT_CUTOFF over a cutoff 336 hours away.
findings.why_it_matters: This breaks the message lifecycle exactly in the middle. An item can be 'sent' and never become 'available', because nothing except a brand-new committed event can add an actor to an event's audience -- and the one mechanism designed to produce that event, pending_progression, is unreachable precisely for the person the item has not reached yet. The world states a process it says will happen, code records the claim as provenance, and then at the moment that process was supposed to happen code asks the world nothing. trajectory.py:872-885 names this run by name as the motivating defect ('a cold email jumped its entire fortnight in a single record after one step'); the newest corpus still does it, so the fix that was added did not address the cause.
findings.suggested_fix: On a K_WAKE firing with provenance world_process, put the question back to the world unconditionally -- 'you said this would happen by now; what concretely has become of it?' -- rather than only when the actor already has an available-unobserved item.

findings.title: 'One pending wake per (actor, about, provenance), replaced not stacked' is violated for actor_plan and over-applied for world_process
findings.evidence: The key is (actor_id, about, provenance) at trajectory.py:205, but 'about' is at the wrong granularity in both directions. For actor plans it is f"plan:{out['call_id']}" (trajectory.py:538) -- unique per call, so pending_wakes always misses and the replacement branch at lines 208-213 is unreachable. Deterministic reproduction with the repository's own scripted transport: 41 actor turns produced 41 scheduled wakes, 41 distinct keys and 0 event.cancelled records. In real runs, reconstructing the queue from the ledger gives a peak of 10 simultaneously queued actor_plan wakes for 'bea' in simulations_v4/case3_group at 2026-10-09T13:15, 9 for 'ines' and 7 for 'kwame'; simulations_v4/a2_r1 contains zero event.cancelled records at all. For world wakes 'about' is trigger_kind (trajectory.py:397) -- a category of trigger, not a subject -- so unrelated processes collide: in case3_group 78 of 214 world-proposed wakes (36%) were silently dropped on that key, and only 1 drop in the entire v4 corpus was for the legitimate beyond-cutoff reason. Concrete collision residue in simulations_v4/a2_r1/grounded_wakes.jsonl: at 2026-09-11T12:00 dana_whitfield holds three near-identical live wakes (plan:c92 due 16:00, actor_intention due 14:00, event_consequence due 14:00), all of which say 'check for venue replies'.
findings.why_it_matters: The two failure modes are opposite and both harmful. Stacking is the pathology the design says it deleted: a person is woken repeatedly off plans they made turns ago, with nothing new to look at, which is a poll authored by the model instead of by code. Over-coalescing silently discards genuinely distinct future processes -- a further-out wake for a different subject is dropped whenever any nearer wake sharing that actor's trigger category is pending -- which removes scheduled future the world explicitly asked for. Neither existing test detects either: tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1601-1625 exercises only the world path (where the coarse key hides the bug) and asserts distinct scheduling times rather than pending depth, and tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1735-1743 asserts len(wakes) <= traj.actor_calls, which is trivially true when every call schedules exactly one wake, so its stated intent ('one is pending at a time, not a queue of them') is unenforced.
findings.suggested_fix: Key actor_plan wakes on the actor alone (or on the subject the actor named, not the call id) so a newer plan replaces the older one, and key world_process wakes on the event ids the wake concerns rather than on trigger_kind.

findings.title: 85% of actor turns are presented as a bare 'time has passed, reconsider'
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/views.py:39-40 defines ELAPSED_TIME_REASON = 'time has passed and you are looking at your situation again', used as the fallback at views.py:66-67 whenever actor_step is called without trigger_event_ids. Only two of the seven actor_step call sites pass them (trajectory.py:631-632 and 859); the wake handler (976, 991, 993), _hand_back_the_turn (606), the completion hand-back (704), the ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED handoff (322) and the last-call sweep (892) all pass none. Measured over every actor_views.jsonl: 654 of 765 rendered views (85%) carry only that line under 'WHAT HAS CHANGED SINCE YOUR LAST TURN' -- 191/215 in simulations_v4, 404/451 in simulations_v3, 59/99 in matched_pairs.
findings.why_it_matters: The design's claim that there are no automatic 'time passed, reconsider' wakes is true of the provenance field in the ledger and false of what actually reaches the person. Combined with the actor_plan stacking above, an actor can be woken ten times off their own stale plans and told nothing on any of them, which is indistinguishable from the widening poll that was deleted -- and it is why so many turns read 'No new information or tasks have emerged, so I will continue with my day as usual' (simulations_v4/case1_cold_email/trajectory.md, mark_cuban at 14:05).
findings.suggested_fix: For an actor_plan wake, render the actor's own stated reason back to them -- it is their own words and therefore not new information -- so the turn says what they came back for instead of only that time has passed.

findings.title: The last-call sweep fires once, wherever the queue first empties, and cannot fire again
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:184 (last_call = {'done': False}) and 886-893: the first time the queue empties before the cutoff, every actor is consulted once with force=True and the flag is latched; every later empty queue breaks straight out to finish(''), which advances to the cutoff (807-815) and permits NO_AT_CUTOFF. In simulations_v4/case1_cold_email that single sweep happened at 2026-07-27T14:05, five minutes into a 336-hour window, and both actors were given empty views. Across simulations_v4, six of nine runs have their last committed event within the first hour of their window (a1_r1 0.0%, b1_r1 0.1%, b1_r2 0.9%, b2_r1 0.0%, b2_r2 0.0%, case1_cold_email 0.0% of the window lived), and b2_r1, b2_r2 and case1_cold_email answer NO_AT_CUTOFF on that basis.
findings.why_it_matters: The sweep exists to make sure a run does not go quiet because nobody was asked, but latching it to the first empty queue means the guarantee is spent at whatever instant that happens to be -- typically minutes into a multi-day window, before anyone has anything to react to. After it is spent the scheduler has no way back, so an empty queue at hour 1 and an empty queue at hour 300 are treated identically. I leave the honesty of the resulting terminal answers to the terminal-independence reviewer; the scheduling defect is that the run stops for want of a wake, not for want of anything happening.
findings.suggested_fix: Allow the sweep to re-arm whenever simulated time has advanced materially since the last one (or replace it entirely with the missing known_deadline wake, which is the grounded version of the same idea).

findings.title: A stale comment claims a return mechanism that no longer exists, concealing a real gap
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:596-600: 'For them, time passes instead, on the widening interval -- which is what being deep in something looks like from outside.' _hand_back_the_turn (591-609) does nothing whatsoever for an actor for whom _has_learned_something is false: no wake is scheduled and no consultation is queued. The widening interval it refers to was deleted.
findings.why_it_matters: The comment reads as though a person deep in their own task has a return path. They do not: unless they themselves scheduled a next_wake on their last turn, they are never consulted again. That is the residue of the 'actors disappear before deadlines' defect and the comment hides it from anyone auditing this function.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the sentence and state plainly that an actor with no plan of their own has no return path, or give them one.

findings.title: Dead assignment after the own-doing observation transition
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:943: rec = dict(rec, observed=did in envelope['for']). _after_commit reads only rec['seq'] and rec['event_id'] (lines 632, 645, 667, 669, 674) and takes its observation decision from envelope, not rec, at line 626.
findings.why_it_matters: Nothing breaks today, but the line looks as though it feeds the post-commit rule and does not, which is the kind of thing that makes a later change to _after_commit silently wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop the assignment, or make _after_commit read rec['observed'] if that was the intent.

findings.title: Wake delays are almost entirely round numbers
findings.evidence: Across all 922 wakes in the three corpora, 835 (91%) fall on an exact hour or quarter-hour multiple; 2 hours (207), 24 hours (162), 1 hour (122) and 30 minutes (130) account for 67% on their own. No code selects these values -- _schedule_wake at trajectory.py:201 parses whatever duration string the model wrote -- so this is model tempo, not a code-imposed schedule, and there is no doubling ladder anywhere.
findings.why_it_matters: It is not a correctness defect and I do not weigh it as one, but the record does not read like people choosing when to come back to things; it reads like a model reaching for round intervals, which is what the deleted geometric poll also looked like from the outside.
findings.suggested_fix: No code change; worth noting in the world and actor prompts that a time to come back is a specific moment in that person's day, not a round interval.
